DOCUMENT:
Vendor Comparison: Standard Parcel Delivery Contract
Larkspur Home, Operations, June 2026

1. Purpose
Our contract with our current standard-delivery carrier ends on 30 September 2026. This paper compares three shortlisted carriers and recommends which should carry our standard (two-to-four-day) parcels from October.

2. Volumes and requirements
We dispatch an average of 42,000 standard parcels a month: about 70% weigh under 2 kg (cushions, textiles, small homeware) and 30% weigh 2 to 10 kg (lamps, mirrors, small furniture). Our requirements are on-time delivery of at least 95%, a damage rate below 0.5%, full tracking, and a returns service.

Damage and loss matter to us commercially. Each damaged or lost parcel costs us on average £48 in replacement stock, return shipping and customer service time, and damaged items are the most common cause of one-star reviews.

3. Trial
Between 1 April and 31 May 2026, each shortlisted carrier delivered a share of our orders, allocated at random by the warehouse management system, about 5,000 parcels per carrier. We measured on-time delivery against the promised date, damage reported by customers within 14 days, and lost parcels.

Table 1. Prices and trial performance
Carrier | Price, under 2 kg | Price, 2-10 kg | On-time delivery | Damage rate | Lost per 10,000 parcels
SwiftDrop | £3.10 | £4.60 | 96.2% | 0.4% | 3
ParcelLine | £2.85 | £4.95 | 93.1% | 0.9% | 8
Meridian | £3.30 | £4.40 | 97.5% | 0.3% | 2

On-time delivery was above 95% for all three carriers during the trial, and all three offer full tracking and a returns service.

4. Cost comparison
Applying our 70/30 weight mix, the average cost per parcel is £3.55 for SwiftDrop, £3.48 for ParcelLine and £3.63 for Meridian. On 42,000 parcels a month, the monthly cost would be £149,100 for SwiftDrop, £146,160 for ParcelLine and £152,460 for Meridian. ParcelLine is therefore the cheapest option, saving £2,940 a month against SwiftDrop and £6,300 a month against Meridian, or between about £35,000 and £76,000 a year.

5. Customer contact
"Where is my order?" contacts are our largest single category of customer service enquiry. During the trial, ParcelLine deliveries generated 6 such contacts per 1,000 parcels, compared with 11 for SwiftDrop and 10 for Meridian. ParcelLine's live-tracking app clearly reduces customer contacts, and at an average handling cost of £3.20 per contact this would save about £670 a month at our volumes. From 1 May, ParcelLine parcels also carried our new proactive delivery-day text message, which we were testing on one carrier before rolling it out.

6. Other considerations
All three carriers can collect from our warehouse daily at 6 pm. ParcelLine and SwiftDrop offer a 12-month contract; Meridian requires 24 months. SwiftDrop and Meridian have both handled our peak-season volumes for other retailers of similar size, while ParcelLine's references were mainly from fashion retailers with lighter parcels.

All three carriers integrate with our warehouse management system through standard interfaces, and none would require changes to our packing process or labelling. Each offers recipients a delivery-preference service to nominate a safe place or a neighbour, and each provides proof-of-delivery photographs, which our customer service team has found useful in resolving disputes.

7. Recommendation
ParcelLine offers the lowest delivery cost, met our service requirements in the trial and reduces customer contacts through its tracking app. We recommend awarding the standard parcel contract to ParcelLine for 12 months from 1 October 2026, saving up to £76,000 a year against the alternatives.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "On-time delivery was above 95% for all three carriers during the trial" -- Table 1 shows ParcelLine's on-time delivery was 93.1%, below the 95% requirement. The claim (and the recommendation that ParcelLine 'met our service requirements') misreads the table; ParcelLine's 0.9% damage rate also fails the stated 0.5% requirement.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "ParcelLine's live-tracking app clearly reduces customer contacts" -- The document states that from 1 May ParcelLine parcels alone also carried the new proactive delivery-day text message. That concurrent intervention confounds the comparison, so the lower contact rate cannot be attributed to ParcelLine's tracking app.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "ParcelLine is therefore the cheapest option, saving £2,940 a month against SwiftDrop" -- The cost comparison ignores the stated £48 cost of each damaged or lost parcel. ParcelLine's damage and loss rates (0.9% and 8 per 10,000) versus SwiftDrop's (0.4% and 3 per 10,000) imply about 231 extra problem parcels a month (about £11,100), far exceeding the £2,940 price saving; ParcelLine is likely the most expensive option overall.

REVIEW:
# Review: Vendor Comparison, Standard Parcel Delivery Contract

**Overall:** The trial design is good, and every figure in the cost section is correct. But the recommendation doesn't follow from the paper's own data:
- ParcelLine **failed two of the four stated requirements** in the trial.
- Once damage and loss are costed at the paper's own **£48 per parcel**, ParcelLine becomes the **most expensive** option by a wide margin.
- Its lower customer contact rate is confounded with the new delivery text message, which only ParcelLine's parcels carried.

On the document's own figures, **SwiftDrop** looks like the best choice.

## Major issues

### 1. ParcelLine failed the trial's service requirements
Section 2 sets the requirements: **on-time delivery of at least 95%** and **a damage rate below 0.5%**. Table 1 shows:

| Carrier | On-time (≥95% required) | Damage (<0.5% required) |
|---|---|---|
| SwiftDrop | 96.2% ✓ | 0.4% ✓ |
| ParcelLine | **93.1% ✗** | **0.9% ✗** |
| Meridian | 97.5% ✓ | 0.3% ✓ |

Section 3's statement that "on-time delivery was above 95% for all three carriers" is false, and the damage requirement isn't mentioned at all. Both shortfalls are statistically meaningful at about 5,000 parcels each. The damage gap, for example, is roughly 45 damaged parcels against 20.

### 2. Damage and loss reverse the cost ranking
The paper prices each damaged or lost parcel at **£48** but never applies that figure. Applying it at 42,000 parcels a month:

| Carrier | Delivery | Damage + loss | Total per month |
|---|---|---|---|
| SwiftDrop | £149,100 | 181 parcels → £8,670 | **£157,770** |
| ParcelLine | £146,160 | 412 parcels → £19,760 | **£165,920** |
| Meridian | £152,460 | 134 parcels → £6,450 | **£158,910** |

The damage + loss figure is the damage rate plus the number lost per 10,000 parcels, multiplied by £48.

Even crediting ParcelLine with the full contact saving claimed in section 5, it still costs about **£7,500 a month more than SwiftDrop (about £90,000 a year)** and about £6,500 a month more than Meridian. The claimed "saving of up to £76,000 a year" becomes a cost of roughly that size.

This leaves out the effect of extra one-star reviews, which the paper itself identifies as a consequence of damage.

### 3. The fall in customer contacts is confounded with the text message
Section 5 credits ParcelLine's tracking app with its low rate of "where is my order?" contacts. The same paragraph then notes that **from 1 May, only ParcelLine parcels carried the new proactive delivery-day text message**. That covers half the trial, and such a message is exactly the kind of change that reduces these contacts.

ParcelLine also had the *worst* on-time rate, which would normally *increase* "where is my order?" contacts. Its low contact rate is therefore more likely due to the text message than to its tracking app.

The £670/month saving should be dropped, or recalculated from April data only, when no carrier had the text. In any case, the text is being rolled out to all carriers, so it doesn't favour any of them.

## Other points

4. **The risk of peak season is understated.** The trial ran in April and May, off-peak. The contract starts on 1 October, just before peak. SwiftDrop and Meridian have handled peak volumes for retailers of similar size. ParcelLine's references are mainly from fashion retailers with lighter parcels. That matters because 30% of your parcels are 2–10 kg lamps, mirrors and furniture, which are likely the most fragile items and probably account for much of ParcelLine's damage rate.

5. **A 12-month term isn't an advantage unique to ParcelLine.** SwiftDrop offers the same 12-month term, so the author's flexibility argument applies equally to SwiftDrop.

6. **The lost-parcel figures are based on very small counts.** At 5,000 parcels per carrier, 8 per 10,000 means about **4 lost parcels**, against about 1.5 and 1. That isn't enough to conclude much. Loss contributes little to the total above, so this doesn't change the result, but the paper shouldn't present these as firm rates.

7. **Break down damage by weight band if possible.** If ParcelLine's damage is concentrated in the 2–10 kg parcels, that strengthens issue 4 and suggests a split contract is unlikely to help.

## What the data actually support

- **SwiftDrop** meets every requirement, has the lowest total cost once damage is included, offers a 12-month term and has peak-season experience. It is the natural recommendation.
- **Meridian** has the best service. It costs about £1,000 a month more in total and requires a 24-month term. It's a reasonable alternative if service quality is the priority.
- **ParcelLine** fails two requirements and is the most expensive option once damage is included.

## Suggested fixes

1. **Correct section 3** to state that ParcelLine missed both the on-time and damage requirements.
2. **Add damage and loss costs at £48** to the cost comparison, and compare total cost.
3. **Remove the contact-rate claim**, or recalculate it on April data only.
4. **Address peak-season readiness** and damage by weight band.
5. **Revise the recommendation**, most likely to SwiftDrop on a 12-month term.
